name: Titan Shroud
geological_features: An opaque upper atmosphere of hydrocarbon haze that blocks all visible light
Estimated 47 moons, most too small to catalog individually
Internal heat source generating more energy than received from the parent star
specific_features: Radio emissions from the deep atmosphere that follow patterns inconsistent with natural storm activity
resources: Helium-3 in the upper atmosphere layers
Moon system offering diverse mining opportunities
description: Titan Shroud is invisible from within its own system. The gas giant's upper atmosphere is a shell of hydrocarbon haze so dense and dark that no light escapes, no light enters, and the planet appears as a perfect black sphere against the stars. Only in infrared does its true nature reveal itself, a world of raging storms and internal heat that outstrips its solar input by a factor of six. The forty-seven known moons orbit a master they have never seen in visible light.

Approaching Titan Shroud is an exercise in sensory deprivation. The haze layer begins hundreds of thousands of kilometers from the visible surface, a gradual dimming that transitions from twilight to absolute darkness over the course of hours. Instruments become the only guide, and even they struggle with the electromagnetic interference from the planet's intense magnetic field. The sense of descending into something alive and aware is reported consistently by pilots who have made the approach.

The radio emissions from the deep atmosphere are Titan Shroud's enduring mystery. They follow repeating patterns with internal structure too organized for storm noise but too irregular for any artificial signal template in the database. Frequency analysis suggests they originate from a layer roughly halfway to the theoretical core, at pressures that would crush any known material. Some researchers have proposed exotic atmospheric chemistry creating resonance effects, while others note that the emissions respond to probe approaches by changing pattern.

The moon system provides Titan Shroud's practical value. Several of the larger moons harbor mineral deposits and water ice, and the outermost moons orbit far enough from the planet to avoid the worst electromagnetic effects. A refueling station on the third moon serves as the primary waypoint for the region, its inhabitants growing accustomed to the permanent dark spot in their sky that is the planet. The radio emissions reach the station on quiet nights, a rhythmic pulse that the crew has learned to sleep through.
